coredata.dc:description: Starch based materials are attractive bio-based alternative to fully synthetic polymers. Native starch has however limited thermoprocessability and properties and must be modified. In order to improve the properties of starch-graft-poly(butyl-acrylate-co-styrene) copolymers via a process as green as possible, we report herein a new method for the dual functionalization of the polysaccharide via a one pot one step reaction in aqueous medium combining free radical polymerizations and ring-opening chemistry. Poly(butyl acrylate) or poly(butyl acrylate-co-styrene) (ca. 60 000 g/mol) and oligo(ε-caprolactone) were grafted on starch with a grafting percentage up to 75 %. The copolymers show two glass transition temperatures: one around 55−60 °C related to starch and a second attributed to the grafted vinyl polymers, from −46 °C to 20 °C depending on butyl acrylate/styrene ratio. The resulting dual functionalized materials exhibit excellent mechanical properties, with elongation at break in the range 20–210 %, while single functionalized starch shows less than 5 %.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Starch based materials are attractive bio-based alternative to fully synthetic polymers. Native starch has however limited thermoprocessability and properties and must be modified. In order to improve the properties of starch-graft-poly(butyl-acrylate-co-styrene) copolymers via a process as green as possible, we report herein a new method for the dual functionalization of the polysaccharide via a one pot one step reaction in aqueous medium combining free radical polymerizations and ring-opening chemistry. Poly(butyl acrylate) or poly(butyl acrylate-co-styrene) (ca. 60 000 g/mol) and oligo(ε-caprolactone) were grafted on starch with a grafting percentage up to 75 %. The copolymers show two glass transition temperatures: one around 55−60 °C related to starch and a second attributed to the grafted vinyl polymers, from −46 °C to 20 °C depending on butyl acrylate/styrene ratio. The resulting dual functionalized materials exhibit excellent mechanical properties, with elongation at break in the range 20–210 %, while single functionalized starch shows less than 5 %.

ce:section.ce:para: Research towards biobased and biodegradable polymers has received much attention this last decade, due notably to environmental concerns and the depletion of oil resources (Chen, Kamitakahara, & Edgar, 2020; Imre, García, Puglia, & Vilaplana, 2019). In this context, starch is a promising starting material due to its availability and low cost that has been the subject of numerous studies (Chen et al., 2015; Fan & Picchioni, 2020). However, starch has limited thermoprocessability along with a strong hydrophilic character and poor mechanical properties as compared to conventional synthetic polymers (Avérous & Halley, 2009). Starch can be plasticized with external plasticizers such as polyols (Lourdin, Coignard, Bizot, & Colonna, 1997)and urea/formamide combinations (Xiaofei, Jiugao, & Jin, 2004) notably. However, some shortcomings, as plasticizer migration, induce an evolution of its properties over time and thus limit its applications.

To overcome some of these drawbacks, the polysaccharide can be blended with synthetic polymers (Wang, Yang, & Wang, 2003), functionalized to yield starch esters and ethers (Aburto, Alric, & Borredon, 1999; Shogren, 2003) or grafted with a polymer (Cazotti et al., 2020; Haq et al., 2020; Meimoun et al., 2018). Graft copolymerization is a very versatile way of functionalization allowing access to materials displaying a combination of the properties of the synthetic polymer and of the starch (Jyothi, 2010). In particular, the radical graft copolymerization can lead to starch-based materials with interesting properties. In this frame, the synthesis of starch-graft-poly(butyl acrylate-co-styrene) copolymers by free-radical graft polymerization was conducted on native starch (Meshram, Patil, Mhaske, & Thorat, 2009), acetylated starch (Mou, Li, Wang, Fei, & Liu, 2012) starch and on dextrin (David et al., 2019). Starch can also be modified by grafting polyesters on its backbone by Ring-Opening Polymerization (ROP) in organic solvents (Chen et al., 2005; Rutot-Houzé et al., 2004) and in water (Choi, Kim, & Park, 1999), a tin based catalyst being used for this purpose.

The combination of the two processes, i.e. radical and ring-opening grafting onto polysaccharides can give access to advanced materials with applications such as drug and fragrance containers or stimuli responsive materials (Chang, Yamabuki, Onimura, & Oishi, 2008; Liu, Huang, Pang, Han, & Ji, 2015; Yan et al., 2009). Diblock copolymers were grafted onto cellulose by combining in a sequential way ROP and Atom Transfer Radical Polymerization (ATRP), involving the use of copper halide, amine ligands and, in the examples reported herein, 2-bromopropionyl bromide (Berthier, Herrmann, & Ouali, 2011; Östmark, Nyström, & Malmström, 2008). In these studies, polyester is grafted as the first block by ROP of a cyclic ester, eventually after a first protection step of a part of the hydroxyl groups. The polymer chain end is further derivatized to yield an initiator for the controlled radical polymerization of a second monomer, leading to the second block.

The dual functionalization, i.e. the grafting of two different oligo/polymers was reported onto cellulose powder and cellulose derivatives such as hydroxyethylcellulose or cellulose diacetate by a multistep procedure involving the grafting of the controlled radical polymerization initiator (Chang et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2015; Vlček et al., 2008). As a representative example, the radical macroinitiator is formed at the first step by the reaction of hydroxyl groups with 2-bromopropionyl bromide in a mixture of tetrahydrofuran (THF) and trimethylamine. The tin-catalyzed ring-opening polymerization of ε-caprolactone initiated by the remaining hydroxyl groups is then realized in xylene, followed by the ATRP of N,N-dimethylaminoethyl methacrylate in THF in the presence of N,N,N’,N’’,N’’-pentamethyldiethylenetriamine (PMDETA) and cupper bromide (CuBr) (Yan et al., 2009).

The combination of radical and ROP processes was, as far we know, reported onto cellulose but never onto starch. The synthetic strategies reported in the literature involve multistep procedures, the use of organic solvents (e.g. THF, xylene), harmful compounds for the initiation of the controlled radical polymerization (e.g.. copper halide, brominated derivatives) and tin-catalyzed ring-opening polymerization. In order to improve the properties of starch-graft-poly(butyl acrylate-co-styrene) copolymers, we developped in this contribution a greener process for the dual functionalization of polysaccharide via free-radical graft polymerization and ring-opening functionalization, using phosphoric acid as organocatalyst for the latter, and a one pot one step process in aqueous medium. The new bi-functionalized materials developped herein exhibit remarkable elongations at break, highlighting promising potentialities for stretchable films. The microstructure of copolymers is studied by Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR), Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FT-IR), Size Exclusion Chromatography (SEC), Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and Thermal Gravimetric Analysis (TGA).
The Materials and Characterization procedures are presented in the Appendix A in Supplementary material.

For all reactions, dry starch (30 g) was gelatinized in 120 ml of water by heating at 95 °C for 30 min. The temperature was then decreased to 85 °C. This leads to the disappearance of the granular structure of starch. The chains are then more accessible for the grafting.

Sodium peroxydisulfate (1 mol % vs. starch) previously dissolved in 10 ml of water, butyl acrylate (BA) and/or styrene (St) (70−75 wt % vs. starch) were added dropwise for 1 h. The grafting polymerization was carried out for 30 additional minutes. A few experiments carried out under inert atmosphere to avoid oxygen led to similar grafting ratio and microstructures than those conducted under air. The latter experimental conditions were thus chosen for the work.
Phosphoric acid (1 mol % vs. ε-caprolactone), ε-caprolactone (CL) (25 wt % vs. starch) were added dropwise for 1 h. The grafting polymerization was carried out for an additional 4 h.

ce:section.ce:section-title: One pot one step free radical and ring-opening grafting
ce:section.ce:para: Sodium peroxydisulfate (1 mol % vs. starch) and phosphoric acid (1 mol % vs. ε-caprolactone) previously dissolved in 10 ml of water were added dropwise for 1 h via dropping funnel. At the same time, monomers, butyl acrylate and/or styrene (70−75 wt % vs. starch) and ε-caprolactone (25−30 wt % vs. starch) were added dropwise for 1 h via a second dropping funnel. The grafting polymerization was carried out for an additional 4 h.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Sequential free radical and ring-opening grafting
ce:section.ce:para: Sodium peroxydisulfate (1 mol % vs. starch) previously dissolved in 10 ml of water, butyl acrylate and/or styrene (70−75 wt % vs. starch) were added dropwise for 1 h. The grafting polymerization was carried out for an additional 30 min. Then, phosphoric acid (1 mol % vs. ε-caprolactone), ε-caprolactone (25−30 wt % vs. starch) were then added dropwise for 1 h. The grafting polymerization was carried out for an additional 4 h.

At the end of the reaction, for each process, the solution was poured in acetone and left during 24 h under magnetic stirring to remove the ungrafted polymer. The product was filtered and dried overnight. The procedure of purification was validated on a few samples by Soxhlet extraction in chloroform during 24 h that led to the same ratio.

The weight grafting percentage (GP) was determined by gravimetry as following:
GP = [(weight copolymer – weight of starch) / weight of starch] × 100
= [weight of grafted polymer / weight of starch] × 100

ce:section.ce:section-title: Syntheses of starch-graft-poly(butyl acrylate) and starch-graft-oligo(ε-caprolactone): single starch functionnalization
ce:section.ce:para: Entries representative of the grafting reactions starting from butyl acrylate and ε-caprolactone on starch via the different routes are presented in Table 1 . Brönsted acid catalysis using phosphoric acid was chosen for the ring-opening since the molecule is harmless at low concentration (it is found in sodas) and it was already used successfully by some of us to graft oligo(ε-caprolactone) on dextran and methylated cellulose in aqueous medium (Stanley et al., 2014). Radical and ring-opening functionalizations were first assessed separately. The free radical graft copolymerization of butyl acrylate in water (entry 1) leads to an almost quantitative efficiency, as reported previously (David et al., 2019). Rather long chains are grafted, with a number-average molecular weight of 80 300 g/mol, and a significant dispersity. The resulting degree of substitution (DS) is consequently low, around 0.0014.

Regarding the mechanism, the decomposition of potassium persulfate in aqueous medium containing an alcohol is described in the literature (Bartlett & Cotman, 1949). The formation of only °CH2OH radicals in methanol has been confirmed by Electron Spin Resonance (Norman, Storey, & West, 1970). Indeed, radicals are more likely located on the carbon in α position of the oxygen rather than on the oxygen, and are more stable on more substituted carbons (Giese, 1986). Thus, it is likely that the functionalization occurs preferentially on the carbons located on the sugar ring. Considering this, we propose the initiation mechanism presented in Scheme 1 (the position 3 has been chosen arbitrarily).

The grafting conducted by ring-opening of the cyclic ester leads to a more modest grafting ratio (entry 2). 1H NMR analysis shows that the grafted chains are composed on average of a single caproyl unit (number-average degree of polymerization estimated at 1.02, Appendix D in Supplementary material), providing a starch hydroxyester compound. This result can be explained by the use of water as the solvent of the reaction, which can either initiate the ROP of ε-caprolactone or enable polycondensation via hydroxyacids resulting from the hydrolysis of the lactone (Scullion & Zinck, 2012), both routes leading to the formation of oligomers or polymers that are not grafted to the polysaccharide. To improve the yield and DP, it would have been interesting to use less water or remove it during the reaction but in this case the viscosity of the medium would be too important. It should be noted that the lactone conversion is quantitative (1H NMR analysis given in the Appendix E in Supplementary material). The resulting DS is ca. 20 times higher than the one obtained by the radical route, around 0.022 in these experimental conditions.

Regarding the grafting mechanism, one can either expect (i) a nucleophilic attack of the carbohydrate hydroxyl on the lactone catalyzed by phosphoric acid, or (ii) the aforementioned hydrolysis of the lactone followed by a condensation reaction between the so formed hydroxyacid and the carbohydrate hydroxyl. This is represented in Scheme 2 . Regarding the regioselectivity, we know from our previous work (Miao et al., 2013) that both primary and secondary carbohydrate hydroxyls can be engaged in a transesterification reaction with ε-caprolactone in the presence of phosphoric acid moieties. If the pathway (i) is the main mechanism, then we do not expect the reaction to be regiospecific. For the condensation pathway (ii), primary alcohols are known to be more reactive in esterification reactions than secondary alcohols. Thus, if this pathway (ii) is the main mechanism, it is likely that primary alcohols are more involved than secondary alcohols.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Syntheses of starch-graft-[poly(butyl acrylate)/oligo(ε-caprolactone)]: dual functionnalization
ce:section.ce:para: In particular, the -CH 2 signal of the poly(butyl acrylate) backbone is split into three due to the presence of both meso and racemic diads (Brar, Kumar, & Kaur, 2002). The caproyl and butyl acrylate signals are overlapping due to the similarity of the molecules, even if a CH2-CH 2-CH2 caproyl signal can be evidenced around 1.4 ppm (shown by the arrow in Fig. 1). Signals representative of caproyl units can also be seen on the 13C NMR spectra of the compounds given in Appendix C in Supplementary material. Both butyl acrylate and ε-caprolactone are thus grafted, showing that the two reactions can occurs simultaneously in water, and validating the proof of our concept. If the overall grafting percentage is similar to entry 1, the grafting ratio of the lactone is significantly improved, by a factor 4. Experiments conducted without the starch (reported Appendix F in Supplementary material) show that this increase of the grafting efficiency may neither be due to a radical grafting of poly(butyl acrylate) on oligo(ε-caprolactone) nor to a transesterification between acrylate and caproyl units. It may thus be attributed to the hydrophobic character of the PBA grafts which could lead to an increase in the lactone and/or oligo(ε-caprolactone) concentration in the vicinity of the polysaccharide. The combination of the two chemistries leads to PBA grafts that are significantly shorter than those obtained by the single radical process. Regarding ε-caprolactone, the hydrolyzed grafts were found to be soluble in the aqueous phase containing the hydrolyzed starch chains and thus could not be isolated. This is likely due to a very low number-average degree of polymerization, that can be expected considering the order of magnitude of 1 found by 1H NMR for a single ring-opening grafting (entry 2).

Experiments combining radical and ring-opening routes were also conducted consecutively, in a two steps reaction, for the sake of comparison. One can start either by the radical route or by the ring-opening one. We obtained significant grafting ratios for the consecutive process starting from the free radical grafting reported entry 4. A slightly higher grafting ratio is obtained, with a lower amount of cyclic ester, leading to a lower DS. The molecular weight of the graft is in the same order of magnitude, yet slightly lower. The two steps consecutive reactions starting from ring-opening followed by radical grafting led to poor results and will not be discussed here.

Even if the DS is low, the process can be considered viable as high GP and M n grafted are obtained for vinyl grafted. The grafting ratio of oligo(ε-caprolactone) is improved by 4 via the combination of two routes of polymerization in aqueous medium compared to ROP alone.

The combination of radical and ring-opening grafting was then realized using styrene as a comonomer with butyl acrylate for the radical polymerization. The insertion of styrene into poly(butyl acrylate) is expected to have an impact on the properties of the resulting materials, by e.g. modulating the thermal and mechanical properties. Representative results are given entries 6 and 9 in Table 2 together with the reactions conducted in the sequential way (7 and 10) and via the single radical route (5 and 8) for comparison.

The copolymers were analyzed by FT-IR (spectra in the Appendix H in Supplementary material). The presence of the bands at 1730 cm-1 (ν(C=O)), at 1250 cm−1 (ν(C-O)), and at 700 cm-1 (deformation of aromatic function) are characteristic of the butyl acrylate, caproyl and styrene groups respectively. The stretching frequencies for νas(CH3) and νs(CH3) (corresponding to methyl of butyl chain) are observed at 2960 and 2872 cm−1, respectively.

DSC analyses carried out on the grafted copolymers at 50 % relative humidity (thermograms in the Appendix I in Supplementary material) reveal two glass transition temperatures (Tg) for all samples involving the radical process, that are given in Tables 1 and 2. The Tg at −46 °C observed for entries 1, 3 and 4 corresponds to the Tg of poly(butyl acrylate). The second Tg is found around 55–59 °C for all samples, whatever the composition of the grafts, and is attributed to the glass transition of the starch backbone. The starch alone has indeed a Tg around 60 °C in similar conditions. When styrene is used as a comonomer for the radical process, the low Tg found around 2 °C (entries 5–7) and 19 °C (entries 8–10) increases with increasing amount of styrene, the Tg of polystyrene being around 100 °C. The presence of a single Tg for poly(butyl acrylate-co-styrene) grafted chains confirms a statistical microstructure which can be expected from the reactivity ratios of the two monomers, rSt 0.73−0.87 and rBA 0.17−0.30 (Fernandez-Garcia et al., 2000). The thermograms did not show oligo(ε-caprolactone) glass transition or melting temperatures, which can be ascribed to the low grafting ratio and the short size of the grafts. The observation of two Tg by DSC is an indication of a phase separation between starch and the grafted polymer, which was already observed by us on starch-graft-poly(butyl acrylate) and starch-graft-polystyrene copolymers in the form of two co-continuous phases (transmission electron microscopy analyses, David et al., 2019).

TGA analyses were performed on the graft copolymers (Tables 1 and 2, curves in the Appendix J in Supplementary material). On all products, evaporation of water (contained in starch) below 100 °C is observed. The unmodified starch substrate starts to degrade around around 250 °C. Two main degradation stages are observed on the copolymers: degradation of the starch part from 250 °C and degradation of grafted chains from 340 °C (entries 1–4) or 350 °C (entries 5–10). Adding styrene units on the copolymer increases the stability of the grafting chains. The short grafts of oligo(ε-caprolactone) may degrade on the same stage as that of starch. Indeed, for example starch acetates degrade in one stage of decomposition, the degradation being shifted towards higher temperatures with increasing DS (Wang et al., 2008).

Mechanical tests were then performed at 50 % relative humidity and room temperature. The results are presented in Table 1 (entries 1–4) and Fig. 2 A (entries 5–10). The temperature at which the mechanical tests were conducted is thus above the Tg of the grafted chains, which are as a consequence at the rubbery state, except for entries 8–10 where the Tg of the grafted chains is around 20 °C, and below the Tg of the starch. The copolymers obtained via single free-radical grafting copolymerization exhibit modest mechanical properties, with a stress at break around 0.3 MPa and an elongation at break close to 1.6 % (entry 1). The replacement of one third butyl acrylate by styrene in the feed allows to increase these properties to 8.7 MPa and 4.4 %, respectively, for the starch-graft-poly(acrylate-co-styrene) copolymer of entry 5. If the combination of the radical and ring-opening routes has a modest effect when butyl acrylate is used as a single radical monomer (entries 3 vs. 1), it leads to an impressive increase of the elongation at break when performed in the presence of 25 % styrene (entries 6 vs. 5), by a factor as high as 17. When the radical grafting is performed with an equimolar amount of styrene and acrylate, the combination of the processes leads in turn to an increase of the stress at break from 6.6 to 7.4 MPa (entries 9 vs. 8), with a smooth increase of the elongation at break. The sequential route leads to similar results, with however a lower elongation at break (entry 7 vs. 6).

Both routes lead to similar performances in terms of GP, M n, and thermal properties. The simultaneous route leads in turn to higher elongation at break. The promising results obtained in entry 6 (BA/St/CL 50/25/25, ε = 75 %) prompted us to go further in this direction.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Final adjustment of feed ratio: optimization of the mechanical behaviour
ce:section.ce:para: A fine modification of the feed was realized in order to assess the effect of the composition on the mechanical properties in this range. The results are reported in Table 3 and Fig. 2B (the mechanical curves are presented in the Appendix K in Supplementary material).

The fine variation of the monomer ratios has neither a substantial influence on the grafting percentages (68–73 %), nor on the molecular weight distributions of the polyvinyl grafts (M n values 62 000–66 000 g/mol and dispersities 2.6–3). The Tg of the grafted chains was found to be below 0 °C whatever the ratios. Mechanicals tests performed on these materials reveals elongations at break from ca. 20 % up to 207 % in this composition range (Fig. 2B) The composition leading to the higher elongation (BA/St 55/20) was assessed without the lactone, leading to a value of 14 %. An increase factor of ca. 15 is thus confirmed while combining the two grafting processes for making the dual functionalized material. It is worth noting that the grafting of a small quantity of oligo(ε-caprolactone) allows to access to thermoplastic resins with interesting mechanical properties.

The visual observation of the specimen during the tensile test reported in Fig. 3 may bring some explanations of the phenomenon. Among the hypotheses able to explain the drop of elongation observed, a necking process during uniaxial tensile tests is clearly disregarded since there is no significant reduction in the section of the specimen located during the deformation. It can be seen that the specimens with high deformations whiten during tensile test. This bleaching is even more noticeable as the film is transparent before the test. It could be ascribed to the formation of cavities. In fact, cavitation is manifested by an increase in the inelastic volume and by a modification of the optical properties of the material (bleaching). The deformation profile, where a decrease in the maximum stress during the plastic deformation is observed, is also in agreement with cavitation phenomenons. The elongation at which the fracture occurs depends on the distribution of these cavities, i.e. localized or in the whole material, and on the number of these cavities. The volume of deformation increases because of the creation of micro-voids while the shear operates without volume variation (Mikus et al., 2014). A more deep study is however necessary to confirm this hypothesis, and will be the subject of a forthcoming paper.

The dual functionalization of a starch is reported in a one pot one step route in aqueous medium, by combining free radical and ring-opening chemistries. Starch-graft-[poly(butyl acrylate)/oligo(ε-caprolactone)] and starch-graft-[poly(butyl acrylate-co-styrene)/oligo(ε-caprolactone)] copolymers were synthesized using sodium peroxydisulfate as radical initiator and phosphoric acid as organocatalyst. Compared to the single ring-opening process, an improvement in the grafting percentage of oligo(ε-caprolactone) is observed, by a factor of 2–4. The DSC analysis showed the presence of two glass transition temperatures, one related to the starch part and the other to the grafted vinyl polymers and being dependent on the butyl acrylate/styrene ratio. Interestingly, the resulting dual functionalized starchs shows elongations at break as high as 210 % (BA/St/CL 55/20/25), a 15 fold increase when compared to the single free radical functionalization. The materials show thus promising potentialities in the field of stretchable films for light occulting applications.
